extracted.intended_audience: students and educated lay readers of natural philosophy/optics and anatomy (late 17th/early 18th-century readership)
extracted.subtask_short: explaining anatomy of bones and sight
extracted.subtask_description: A didactic exposition describing the structure and functions of bones, joints, marrow, and the organs of sight, together with elementary optics (laws of rays, refraction, lens imaging) illustrated by experiments. The text aims to teach how anatomical structures and optical laws cooperate to produce vision and joint motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid applying oil or moisture to exposed bones
rubrics_metrics.description: Skilful surgeons must carefully abstain from the use of all moist and oily matters upon naked (denuded) bones, as such application is 'more pernicious' and causes corruption of the bone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites authorities (Hildanus, Mr. Pare) and empirical surgical experience: oils and liquid medicines improperly applied to exposed bone may produce 'miserable Corruption'. This is given both as medical counsel and as evidence supporting textual analogies (e.g., biblical imagery of 'oil into his bones').

rubrics_metrics.name: Bones are hollow to contain marrow for lubrication and flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Bones were made hollow by design to serve as receptacles of a fat or oleaginous matter (marrow) which renders limbs smooth and supple in motion and prevents cartilage wear by continual attrition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogies made to greased axletrees of wagons and musicians oiling strings; marrow keeps bones and ligaments from becoming brittle and provides necessary moisture. This is presented as both anatomical fact and teleological argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marrow prevents cartilage wear and maintains ligament condition
rubrics_metrics.description: The marrow keeps the ligaments and little bands of bones in proper condition by providing moisture; without it bones would be too dry and brittle and joints would be worn out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical/functionalist explanation: marrow supplies an oily substance that lubricates joint surfaces and preserves flexibility; referenced to observations and prior treatises for experimental support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixture of water and oil can improve motion of mechanical suckers and analogously joint movement
rubrics_metrics.description: A repeated mixture of water and oil on a pump's sucker produces smoother and easier motion than oil or water alone (Boyle's experiments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as an experimental observation (Boyle) and used analogically to explain why a mixture of watery and oily humours in joints may be effective in lubricating articulations; suggests practical experimental method (dip in water then oil, repeat).

rubrics_metrics.name: Joints contain glands and humours that lubricate and are protected by cavities
rubrics_metrics.description: There are perpetual springs/fountains near joints producing an oily marrow and a tough mucilaginous humour which enter the joint between cartilages; glands are placed and protected in cavities to prevent damage from bone movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes anatomical arrangement: glands situated in cavities so they aren't injured by pressing bones; when compressed by motion they yield more liquor, and at rest they retain it. References Dr. Havers and specific figures/tables for experimental evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Glands secrete more lubrication when joints are compressed
rubrics_metrics.description: When joints undergo great inflections and much work, the glands are softly compressed to render their liquor more freely, supplying what the joint then requires; when at rest they preserve more of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains dynamic secretion linked to mechanical compression; offered as explanatory mechanism for how lubrication is regulated according to use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anatomical complexity (glands, humours, cavity protection) supports teleological inference
rubrics_metrics.description: The intricate arrangement of glands, humours, cavities, and motions in joints provides visible tokens of design and the wisdom of the Creator rather than random chance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical/argumentative criterion: complexity and purposive arrangement are marshalled as evidence for design; readers are invited to consider whether such orderliness could arise without intention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eyelids move rapidly to protect the tender eye
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the eye is very tender and easily hurt, the eyelid can be drawn over it with inconceivable swiftness upon the approach of danger and lifted quickly to admit light; this is enabled by particular muscles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functional explanation emphasizing protection and sleep/rest functions; notes the presence of specific muscles enabling prompt action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cartilaginous support of eyelids for speed and tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Eyelids are provided with a cartilaginous bow which keeps them from hanging loose and ensures swifter motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anatomical detail explaining how structure preserves function (prevents flaccidity, aids speed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Eye socket bones protect the globe from pressure/deformation
rubrics_metrics.description: The eye is encompassed on all sides by bones to defend it from outward harms because by the least pressure the figure of the eye would be changed and sight greatly disordered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical test: shut one eye and press the other to notice how pressure distorts vision; structural explanation for orbital bones' function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structures (eyebrows, glands) prevent foreign fluids and keep the eye moist
rubrics_metrics.description: Eyebrows prevent sweat from the forehead flowing into the eyes; glands placed in/around the eye continuously supply a moisture to keep the eye smooth and clear; tears are drained into the nostrils by passages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists multiple protective/moisture-maintaining structures and their purposes (sweat prevention, constant lubrication, tear drainage), including observations on involuntary large tear flows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extraocular muscles allow eye movement without turning the head
rubrics_metrics.description: Different muscles are fastened to the eye so that it can be turned in all directions, sparing the need to turn the head to observe different objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functional/anatomical note highlighting coordination and mechanical advantage of multiple muscles enabling rapid, precise gaze shifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Light propagates spherically from a point and in straight lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Light from a point diffuses its beams spherically; in general rays proceed in straight lines and a dark (opaque) object placed on the ray blocks sight along that line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated with diagrams (rays PC, etc.) and the experiment of placing an opaque body between eye and illuminated point to observe blocking; foundational assumption for subsequent optics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divergent rays must be made convergent to form a distinct image
rubrics_metrics.description: Rays coming from one point of an object diverge; to form a distinct image on the eye (or a screen) these rays must be reconverged to a point (via refraction or lenses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Law of imaging: distinct vision requires that rays from each point be reunited at corresponding points on the retina (or paper), otherwise images are confused; motivates need for refracting media (humours, lenses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Refraction: rays bend when passing obliquely between media of different density
rubrics_metrics.description: When rays pass from one transparent medium into another (air into water, glass, etc.) with oblique incidence they are bent; if they fall perpendicularly they are not bent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained with experiments (candle/coin in basin or vessel) showing apparent displacement of objects when water is added; includes explanation of bending toward the perpendicular when entering denser medium and away when leaving to rarer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perpendicular incidence produces no refraction
rubrics_metrics.description: A ray falling at right angles to the surface between two media suffers no refraction and continues straight through.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiment: view a coin through a narrow perpendicular tube before and after filling the vessel with water—the coin's apparent position remains unchanged if the ray is perpendicular.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convex lenses can make divergent rays converge and form inverted images
rubrics_metrics.description: A convex, spherical glass can inflect diverging rays from a point and unite them again about a point, producing an inverted image (as in spectacles, burning-glasses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes the double refraction through convex glass and demonstrates with candle-to-paper experiments and spectacle lenses producing inverted images at appropriate distances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dark-chamber (camera obscura) demonstrates image formation by small aperture and lens
rubrics_metrics.description: A dark chamber with a small hole (and optionally a convex glass) projects exact, inverted images of external objects onto a white surface inside, showing that images are formed by convergent rays entering a dark cavity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides practical instructions: make chamber dark, leave small round hole, hang white paper to observe images—especially effective when sunlit exteriors contrast with shaded glass.

rubrics_metrics.name: The eye functions as a dark chamber with lens system forming inverted images
rubrics_metrics.description: The eye is a real dark chamber where external images are painted on the bottom (retina) by light passing through transparent membranes and humours, just like a dark chamber with a convex glass; demonstrated with an ox eye experiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental demonstration: make a small hole in the membrane of a warm ox eye and observe an inverted candle image on the inner membranes or on paper placed behind the vitreous humour; precautions about not damaging delicate membranes; observations about image size changing with distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and specific humours/lens curvatures are required for proper focusing
rubrics_metrics.description: The cornea must be a thin, bright, transparent membrane to admit light; the eye's cavities must be filled with appropriately dense/convex media—the aqueous humour (clear, denser than air), the crystalline humour (thicker, convex, acts like lens), and the vitreous humour (transparent, filling the rear cavity)—so that multiple refractions focus rays at the proper point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the necessity of sequential refractions: aqueous refraction first toward each other, then crystalline refraction to collect rays nearer, and the vitreous humour to position the final focus at the retina; each layer's relative density, convexity, and transparency are specified and tied to observed focusing behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple refractions and lens curvatures control image distance and clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: If rays were not refracted appropriately (or if refractions occurred only once), images would form too far behind the eye or would be confused; proper convexities and differing refractive indices ensure the image forms at the right point and with correct size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why a sequence of humours with differing thicknesses and curvatures is necessary to avoid large, confused images; includes practical observation that moving the object nearer enlarges the image and vice versa (used to judge distance by apparent size).
